prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Zenithit

outputs.L1:
I wish I would like a ship  
that all night carries its beloved captain,  
sleeping through no weather,  
slip past dawn  
and wake with nothing  
but strange things  
that did not happen  
to report.

But I get up in the dark  
and parachute quietly down  
to the kitchen  
to begin the purely mental ritual:  
plugging in the useless worry machine.

Above me, she sleeps  
like the innocent, still-dreaming older sister  
to all gentle things.

The white screen impassively asks me  
to say what does not matter does,  
so I shut it down  
and think about the lake  
near where I live.

It’s a lagoon, getting lighter,  
like an old blue, just-switched-on television—  
maybe a Zenith.  
It has two arms.  
They stretch without feeling  
east to embrace an empty park.

A little light;  
then everything has a shadow.  
I almost hear a silent bell,  
low voices.

I brought us to this old city.  
The port connects to the world  
where everyone pretends to know  
they live on an island,  
waiting for the giant wave  
in some form—  
maybe radiation in the yard.

The wind blows.  
The whole black sky looks down  
for an instant  
through my sleepy, isolate frame.  
A complex child-hologram flickers,  
angrily holding a green plastic shovel,  
then disappears,  
leaving an empty column waiting.

Bill, who I knew was so angry,  
is dead.  
Whatever he was going through,  
I kept away.  
I never did anything.

I love his poem.  
He was really good.  
I keep forgetting his last name.  
I always leave his handmade book  
on my desk,  
not to remember,  
but because, for hours after everything,  
everyone says sounds like a language  
I never knew  
but now speak.

Spirit, I know  
you would have hated how I think.  
You would have liked this music  
in another room,  
pushing the alien voice  
into the millennium—  
the one you left so early.

Spirit,  
you were right:  
all noble things are gone,  
except to struggle  
and be loved.
outputs.L2:
I want to be like a vessel  
that moves through the entire night,  
carrying its cherished captain  
asleep, untouched by weather,  
sliding beyond morning,  
then waking with only odd accounts  
of things that never actually occurred.

Instead, I rise before daylight  
and descend softly, as if by parachute,  
into the kitchen,  
to start the entirely inward ceremony  
of connecting the pointless machine of worry.

Above me, she is sleeping,  
blameless,  
like the elder sister still dreaming  
on behalf of everything gentle.

The blank white screen  
asks without emotion  
for me to declare what is irrelevant,  
and because it is irrelevant,  
I turn it off.

Then I think of the lake  
close to my home.  
It is really a lagoon,  
brightening slowly,  
like an old blue television  
just powered on—  
maybe a Zenith.

It has two extensions,  
reaching eastward without sensation  
to hold an empty park.  
A little light arrives,  
and then every object  
casts a shadow.

I almost hear  
a noiseless bell,  
low human voices.

I brought us here  
to this ancient city.  
The harbor joins it  
to the rest of the world,  
where everyone acts as though they understand  
they are living on an island,  
waiting for the enormous wave  
in whatever shape it chooses—  
perhaps radiation in the yard.

The wind moves.  
For one second,  
the entire black sky stares downward  
through my drowsy, separate body.

A complicated child,  
like a hologram, flashes into view,  
furiously gripping  
a green plastic shovel,  
then vanishes,  
leaving behind a vacant column  
as if expecting something.

Bill, whom I knew,  
was filled with anger.  
Now he is dead.  
Whatever he was enduring,  
I stayed away from it.  
I never helped.  
I never did anything.

I love his poem.  
He was truly talented.  
I keep failing to remember  
his last name.

I always keep  
his handmade book  
on my desk—  
not so I can remember,  
but because for hours afterward,  
everything anyone says  
sounds like a language  
I had never learned,  
though now I can speak it.

Spirit, I know  
you would have despised  
the way I imagine  
you might have enjoyed  
this music coming from another room,  
forcing that alien voice  
forward into the millennium  
you abandoned so soon.

Spirit,  
you were correct:  
all noble things have disappeared,  
except the effort to go on  
and the chance to be loved.
outputs.L3:
The poem begins with a wish for peace and surrender. The speaker imagines how comforting it would be to drift through life like a ship moving quietly over water, carrying its sleeping captain safely onward. This image suggests a longing to be released from responsibility, wakefulness, and fear. Instead of such rest, however, the speaker wakes in darkness and enters a familiar ritual of anxious thinking. The mind begins its repetitive work, turning over worries and possibilities before the day has even begun.

The speaker then resists this inward machinery of fear. The “useless worry machine” is rejected as something unproductive and exhausting, a device that generates anxiety without offering solutions. In place of private panic, the speaker turns outward, paying attention to the physical world: the lake, the city, and the peculiar atmosphere of dawn. This shift in focus gives the poem a wider scope. The world outside is not exactly comforting, but it is vivid and real, and it interrupts the speaker’s cycle of obsessive thought.

The city itself is presented as a kind of island or port, surrounded by water and marked by a sense of isolation. It is not merely a setting but a place with its own emotional climate. The people who live there seem to share an unspoken expectation that disaster may arrive at any moment. This feeling of anticipated catastrophe hangs over the city like weather. The port imagery reinforces a sense of waiting: ships may come and go, but the inhabitants remain suspended between ordinary life and the possibility of sudden ruin.

Within this atmosphere, the speaker remembers Bill, a dead poet and acquaintance. The memory introduces a more personal form of unease. The speaker feels guilt for having kept a distance from Bill’s suffering, perhaps out of fear, discomfort, or helplessness. Bill’s death becomes more than a private loss; it becomes a moral challenge. The speaker is forced to confront the limits of sympathy and the painful knowledge that one can fail others by withdrawing when their suffering becomes difficult to face.

The poem closes by addressing Bill’s spirit directly. This final gesture gives the ending an elegiac quality, as if the speaker is trying to speak across the boundary between the living and the dead. Although the poem suggests that certain noble things may have disappeared, it does not end in complete despair. What remains are struggle and love: imperfect, demanding, but still meaningful. The ending acknowledges loss while also affirming that human connection, effort, and care continue even in a damaged world.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a restless meditation at dawn, moving through anxiety, grief, and existential dread in a deliberately fragmented way. It begins in a space of domestic worry, where ordinary morning consciousness is already disturbed by fear, guilt, and unease. From there, the speaker’s mind shifts outward and inward at once: to the image of a lagoon, to the city, to memories of personal and historical loss, and finally to the presence of a dead poet-friend. These movements do not follow a straightforward narrative but instead reflect the unstable motion of thought under emotional pressure.

As the poem develops, private anxiety expands into a broader sense of cultural and spiritual collapse. The speaker feels alienated from the world and burdened by guilt, while the surrounding images suggest decay, apocalypse, and the failure of once “noble things.” Ideals that might once have offered certainty—art, civilization, friendship, moral purpose—appear damaged or insufficient. The city becomes a place of estrangement, memory becomes painful rather than consoling, and the dead friend stands as a reminder of both love and irreparable loss.

Yet the poem does not end in complete despair. Although it acknowledges the fragility of human meaning, it also discovers what remains after certainty has fallen away. The speaker recognizes that struggle itself has value, that love continues to matter even when it cannot prevent suffering, and that connection persists in fragile but real forms. The dead friend is absent, but the act of remembering him becomes a form of continued relationship. In this way, the poem suggests that meaning is not found in grand ideals or permanent assurances, but in the difficult persistence of human attachment, responsibility, and care. Even amid dread and collapse, the poem affirms that love and connection endure as small but essential sources of hope.

**Zenithit**

Zenithit represents the idea of reaching the highest point of progress, clarity, and innovation. Inspired by the word “zenith,” it suggests ambition, excellence, and forward movement. Whether used as a brand name, a technology concept, or a creative project, Zenithit carries a sense of purpose: to rise above limitations and aim for the best possible outcome.

In a business or technology context, Zenithit could symbolize smart solutions designed to help people and organizations grow. It reflects reliability, modern thinking, and a commitment to improvement. A company named Zenithit might focus on digital transformation, software development, consulting, or innovative services that guide clients toward success.

The strength of Zenithit lies in its memorable sound and positive meaning. It feels futuristic while remaining simple and professional. As a concept, it encourages confidence, creativity, and achievement—qualities that are valuable in any field.

Ultimately, Zenithit can be understood as more than just a name. It is a symbol of aspiration: the drive to reach new heights, overcome challenges, and create something meaningful.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a long free-verse poem in the style of a contemporary elegy, with no line breaks shown, about waking before dawn, anxiety, a sleeping partner, a lake or lagoon, apocalypse, memory, and a dead poet friend named Bill.
counterfactuals.output: Before dawn I wake as if summoned by a small animal inside my chest, the one that has never learned any language but alarm, and the room is blue with the hour before evidence, before the kettle, before the first truck on the road, before even the gulls begin their ruined laughter over the lagoon, and beside me you are sleeping with one hand open on the sheet, your face turned slightly away, innocent not because you are innocent but because sleep has taken from you the burden of explaining yourself to the century, and I lie there listening to you breathe as if breath were a form of weather we had not yet destroyed, as if the planet could still be talked down from the ledge by this one soft, repeating proof, in, out, in, out, while the news waits in the black glass of the phone like a bomb trained to recognize my thumb, while the lake beyond the houses lies flat and metallic under the last stars, holding the moon in its mouth, holding the drowned reeds, the plastic bag snagged on a branch, the ghosts of fish, the old reflections of children we were not careful enough to remain, and I think, Bill, you would have known how to stand in this hour without making it beautiful too quickly, you would have coughed into your fist and said something bitter about angels, or empire, or the price of pears, then turned your face toward the water as if receiving instructions from the dead minnows and the cold birds stitching themselves into the gray; Bill, you who died before the fires turned noon into a doctrine, before the maps began to blush with heat, before the word unprecedented became a weather pattern, before the sirens learned our names, I want to tell you the world has continued in its old talent for ending, and yet the garbage trucks still lift their green bins with enormous tenderness, and the bakery still opens at six, and my beloved still sleeps through the first tremor of my mind, and somewhere a child is being carried from one room to another, heavy with dreams, warm as bread, while the future sharpens its teeth in the basement; I wake before dawn and memory comes not as a film but as a weather front, the porch where we drank cheap wine from coffee mugs, your laugh breaking into its own coughing, the notebook you kept in your coat because you said the soul was mostly scraps, the afternoon you read me a poem about your father and afterward we pretended to study the clouds because neither of us could bear the mercy of being seen, the last message I did not answer because I was tired, because the sink was full, because I believed, with the arrogance of the living, that time was a cupboard endlessly restocked; now the unsent tenderness blooms like mold in every corner, now I speak to you in the kitchen while the spoon clicks against the cup, now I ask the empty chair what to do with dread so large it has become domestic, folded into towels, tucked among receipts, sleeping under the bed like a second dog; outside, the lagoon is not yet silver, not yet green, only a dark absence where the world keeps some of its older thoughts, and the reeds stand in the shallows like mourners who have forgotten the name of the dead but not the posture of grief, and the apocalypse is not one thing, not trumpet, not horseman, not bright door torn open in the sky, but the incremental failure of tenderness, the coral whitening like a face under fluorescent light, the forests becoming smoke becoming weather becoming lung, the old men on television selling water back to the thirsty, the children practicing lockdown in rooms decorated with paper suns, the monarchs fewer each year, the bees going quiet, the lakes warming, the passwords expiring, the glaciers withdrawing their long blue bodies from our touch; and still, in the bed beside me, your shoulder rises from the blanket like a small continent spared for another minute, and I love you with a terror so plain it has no metaphor, or only the oldest one, the hand reaching in the dark to confirm the other hand is there; forgive me, Bill, for still wanting coffee, for still wanting the particular, for still being pierced by the orange rind of morning when it finally opens over the water, forgive me for envying your absence from the alerts, the arguments, the poisoned rain, and forgive me too for the cruel thought that you abandoned us to all this light, because grief is selfish before it is holy, and I am still learning how to carry you without making of you a tool, a weather vane, a saint in the museum of my better feelings; I remember the last time we walked by the lake, how the wind worried the surface into scales, how you said every body of water is an unfinished elegy, always receiving, never explaining, and then you picked up a stone and held it so long I thought you might be listening for a heartbeat, and maybe you were, maybe the earth was already telling you something the rest of us could not hear over our plans; now the dawn loosens one pale thread at a time, the room returning to itself, chair, book, glass, your shoes near the door collapsed in their ordinary exhaustion, and anxiety, that bad priest, begins its sermon: what if the test results, what if the bank, what if the border, what if the fever, what if the ocean, what if the election, what if the knock at the door, what if the door itself, what if love is only a temporary shelter built from the materials of loss; but your breathing continues, stubborn metronome, and the lake receives the first bird without comment, and somewhere under the mud the turtles are still dreaming their armored dreams, and the dead, if they are anywhere, are perhaps not beyond us but beneath the day, a root system of voices drinking from the dark; Bill, old friend, dead poet, patron saint of unfinished cigarettes and merciless revisions, come sit with me in this hour before anyone asks us to be useful, come tell me again that despair is a kind of vanity when it refuses the evidence of the ordinary, the spoon, the wrist, the window warming, the heron unfolding from the reeds like a thought the world almost forgot to have; tell me that to remember is not to resurrect and not to bury but to keep walking to the edge of the water with a name in the mouth until the name becomes less wound than lantern; tell me that the apocalypse has always been near, wearing different uniforms, and that our task is not to be unafraid but to keep passing the cup, keep mending the net, keep touching the beloved’s back lightly enough not to wake them, just enough to say, from the far shore of one body to another, I am here, you are here, the morning has not solved anything, the morning has come anyway; and when the sun finally breaks, it does not save us, it merely reveals the floating leaves, the oil-sheen, the egret lifting its knees through the shallows with sacerdotal care, the roofs slick with dew, the world beloved and damaged beyond argument, and I rise quietly, leaving you to sleep a little longer, because there is mercy in letting someone remain uncalled by the day, and in the kitchen I fill the kettle, rinse the cup, watch steam ghost the window, and for one second the glass holds all of it together: my face, your sleeping body behind me, the brightening lagoon, the dead friend leaning in his impossible coat, the ruined century, the small blue flame under the water, or under the kettle, or under the heart, going on, going on, as if continuation itself were a prayer we had forgotten we were allowed to say.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal prose poem about insomnia and grief, moving from a dark kitchen and computer screen to an old city by the water, ending with an address to a dead friend or spirit about struggle and love.
counterfactuals.output:
At three in the morning the kitchen is a country without weather.  
The cups stand in their white cabinets like little skulls, listening.  
A spoon lies in the sink with the exhausted silver of a moon that has fallen  
and cannot be persuaded back into the sky.

The refrigerator hums its green psalm.  
The floor remembers every foot that has crossed it,  
even yours, though you never stood here—  
grief is a locksmith, grief enters any room.

On the table, the computer opens one blue eye.  
Its light pours over my hands, making them look borrowed,  
hands of a diver, a thief, a saint in an x-ray.  
Messages drift upward from the screen like drowned letters:  
names, dates, weather, the small machinery of the living.  
I click and click, as if the dead were hidden in a folder,  
as if the past might ask for a password  
and forgive me for forgetting it.

Outside, the night presses its forehead to the window.  
Inside, insomnia walks in circles wearing your coat.

Then the room loosens. The walls take off their plaster masks.  
The kitchen tiles become black water.  
The cursor blinks into a lighthouse far away,  
and I am walking, without having risen,  
through an old city built at the edge of a harbor.

The streets are narrow as veins.  
Laundry hangs between houses like faded flags of surrender.  
Stone steps climb and descend for no reason.  
Cats slip through alleys with the dignity of prophets.  
Every door has a brass handle polished by generations of leaving.  
The sea is at the end of every street,  
breathing its salt breath through the shutters,  
lifting the boats by their ribs.

In the square, a fountain talks in its sleep.  
Its water spills from the mouth of a fish with human eyes.  
Church bells float above the roofs, dark birds made of bronze.  
Old women cross themselves before bakeries.  
A child runs past carrying a red kite, though there is no wind.  
And everywhere the dead sit quietly at café tables,  
stirring sugar into cups of black air.

I look for you among them.

I look in the harbor, where the moored boats knock together  
like teeth in a fever.  
I look beneath the arcade, where rain has written its long transparent sentences.  
I look in the windows of the closed pharmacy,  
in the green bottles and bandages,  
in the remedies for pain that are never enough.

The city seems to know your name.  
It keeps turning corners before I can ask.  
It folds the map into a paper bird and releases it over the water.  
It leaves your shadow on a bench beside the quay,  
and when I sit there, the shadow is warm.

My friend, my absent one,  
you who went ahead into the room without doors,  
do you still struggle where you are?  
Does the dark have weight?  
Does love arrive there late and out of breath,  
carrying its ridiculous lantern?

I have not learned how to live without speaking to you.  
I keep placing bread on the table for the invisible.  
I keep mistaking the wind for an answer.  
But listen—if listening is still possible:  
we are all wrestling the same angel in different rooms.  
We are all bruised by the wings we cannot see.

If struggle made a language, you were fluent.  
If sorrow were a sea, you crossed it nightly.  
And if love could have held you here,  
if love were rope, or harbor, or hand,  
you would be beside me now, laughing softly  
at the strange blue dawn beginning on the screen.

Still I send it to you:  
this sleepless city, this dark kitchen,  
this heart with its broken hinge, still opening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem with compressed spacing and enjambed phrases, imitating the tone of late 20th-century American poetry, including images of a ship, parachuting to the kitchen, a useless worry machine, a Zenith television, a green plastic shovel, and a forgotten handmade book.
counterfactuals.output:
The ship kept entering the room  
without water—  
its ropes dark with sleep,its bell  
a small bad moon  
I had no use for

and still I was parachuting  
to the kitchen,  
past the wallpaper’s weather,  
past the useless worry machine  
clicking its little teeth  
in the hall

Nobody had invented mercy  
but the Zenith television  
glowed anyway,blue  
as a saint with bad reception,  
telling us the cities  
were burning politely

On the floor a green plastic shovel  
waited for snow,or sand,  
or the grave of some insect  
we had loved  
for one minute  
in July

I opened the drawer  
and found the forgotten handmade book—  
thread spine,thumb-smudged cover,  
pages smelling faintly  
of glue and rain

Inside: no answers,  
only a ship,a kitchen,  
a falling body  
learning the names  
of ordinary objects

as if naming them  
could keep them  
from leaving.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic dawn meditation in free verse from the perspective of someone who wakes up anxious while their partner sleeps, thinks about a nearby lagoon and a dead acquaintance whose poems they admired, and concludes that noble things are gone except struggle and being loved.
counterfactuals.output:
Before the birds begin  
their small, reckless arguments,  
I wake with the old animal in my chest  
turning in its narrow cage.

Beside me, you sleep—  
one hand open on the sheet  
as if you have just let go  
of some harmless, radiant thing.

The room is blue with almost-morning.  
The windows hold their breath.  
Far off, though I cannot see it,  
the lagoon receives the first light  
without surprise.

I think of its dull silver skin,  
the reeds whispering at the edges,  
the slow birds lifting from mud  
like thoughts that have finally forgiven  
the body that kept them.

And I think of him—dead now—  
not a friend exactly,  
but near enough to grief  
that his name still startles me.

How I loved his poems,  
their difficult music,  
the way they stood in the world  
thin and stubborn as winter trees,  
refusing comfort,  
refusing lies.

He is nowhere this morning.  
Or he is in the lagoon,  
in the pale water,  
in the mist loosening itself  
from the reeds.

I lie still  
so I will not wake you,  
though everything in me  
is pacing.

Dawn keeps arriving  
with its cold hands,  
touching the roofs, the floor,  
the cup left empty on the table.

Once I believed in noble things—  
glory, perhaps,  
or the clean shape of a life  
made meaningful by art,  
by courage,  
by some bright discipline of the soul.

But the dead keep dying.  
The poems remain  
and do not save us.  
The lagoon shines  
and does not answer.

So let the noble things be gone.

There is only this:  
the struggle to breathe through fear,  
to rise,  
to go on carrying the name  
of every lost and lovely thing—

and your sleeping body beside me,  
warm in the blue hour,  
loving me  
without knowing  
how much of the world  
it is holding together.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-block poem without punctuation that blends domestic morning routine, ecological/apocalyptic dread, childhood hallucination, guilt over avoiding an angry dead friend, and a final apostrophe to his spirit, in a tender but uneasy voice.
counterfactuals.output:
I wake before the kettle and listen to the house breathe like an animal ashamed of its warmth  
the cups wait in their pale cupboard  
the bread waits under its cloth  
outside the trees hold their small green hands to the light as if begging it not to leave them burning  
I rinse the knife and think of oceans rising in the sink  
of bees gone quiet in the lavender  
of children learning the names of birds from screens after the birds have become weather  
my mother used to hum in the mornings while I saw blue horses stepping through the hallway walls  
their ribs full of stars  
their eyes like wet coins  
I never told her because the day was already too full of cereal and shoes and the bus sighing at the curb  
now I stand in my own kitchen with coffee darkening in the pot  
and I remember how you called after the fight  
how I let the phone ring until your anger fell back into silence  
how later you died with that silence still warm between us  
I have made a habit of small survivals  
laundry folded while forests smoke  
eggs cracked while ice calves into black water  
mail opened while the future gathers its teeth  
and still I avoid the street where you lived  
still I cross myself with errands  
still I say tomorrow I will come and stand where your voice last touched the air  
dear restless one  
dear friend with your furious laugh  
if you are near the window forgive the steam on the glass  
forgive the spoon in my hand  
forgive this morning that keeps asking me to eat  
sit with me if you can  
or haunt me gently  
not because I deserve gentleness  
but because I am finally listening
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
